Where it began

Brendon McCullum was born in Dunedin on 27 September 1981 and went to King's High School in the city. He was a useful rugby player there too, good enough to be picked ahead of a schoolboy called Dan Carter.

Cricket won, and he came through with Otago, where his brother Nathan was a team-mate. He began in the New Zealand side as a wicketkeeper who could bat, and the batting soon took over.

The player

McCullum played 101 Tests from 2004 to 2016, making 6,453 runs at 38.64 with 12 hundreds. As a keeper he held 167 catches and made 11 stumpings, and he took 31 more catches in the field. He captained New Zealand in 31 Tests, winning 11.

His great year was 2014. At the Basin Reserve he made 302 against India, the first triple hundred by a New Zealander, sharing a stand of 352 with BJ Watling to save the match. Before that year was out he had passed 1,000 Test runs in it, something no New Zealander had managed before. In 2015 he led his country to their first World Cup final. Then, in his last Test, at Christchurch in 2016, he reached a hundred in 54 balls, the quickest in Test history at the time, and in the same innings went past Adam Gilchrist for the most Test sixes.

What made him special

McCullum attacked from the first ball. He loved to loft the ball over extra cover and was quick to cut anything short. He scooped fast bowlers over the keeper's head so often that one version of the shot became known as the McScoop. As a captain he played the same way, and his New Zealand side soon shook off any idea that they were easy to beat.

He was never one for a long, quiet vigil at the crease. In 2014 alone he hit 33 Test sixes, which suggests the defensive prod was something he kept for emergencies.

Away from the middle

In the very first IPL match, in 2008, he made 158 not out for Kolkata, and went on to play T20 cricket all over the world. After retiring he coached Kolkata and Trinbago, then England's Test side from 2022, where his attacking approach was nicknamed Bazball after him. From 2025 he also took charge of England's white-ball sides.

He was appointed to the New Zealand Order of Merit as an Officer, won the Sir Richard Hadlee Medal and was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year. Wellington gave him the key to the city, and in 2016 he gave the MCC Spirit of Cricket Cowdrey Lecture.

And finally

He bowled a little too. His one Test wicket was a caught and bowled against Pakistan in 2014, and his best figures, 1 for 1, look very fine indeed on paper.
